query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled ~4 at% Cr substitution into a baseline single‐phase BCC refractory HEA (e.g., HfMoTaTiZr) while simultaneously increasing low-density elements like Ti and Zr will promote the formation of a fine, reticulated Laves phase within the BCC matrix, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility and reducing the overall density compared to the Cr-free alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase BCC refractory HEA (HfMoTaTiZr) that exhibits relatively high density, moderate yield strength (~1543 MPa), and low ductility (~11.6% fracture strain).
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 4 at% Cr into the base composition and adjust elemental ratios to increase the proportion of low-density elements (Ti and Zr) during alloy synthesis via vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed under standard homogenization and heat treatment conditions and then tested at room temperature under compressive loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The targeted formation of a dispersed, reticulated Laves phase (an intermetallic precipitate) within a continuous BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Cr substitution increases lattice distortion and drives limited phase separation, which results in the nucleation of a fine Laves phase that can impede dislocation motion (thus increasing yield strength) while its network structure helps deflect crack propagation (improving ductility). Concurrently, elevating Ti and Zr fractions reduces the alloy’s overall density.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cr-modified alloy is expected to show an increase in yield strength by roughly 200 MPa and an improvement in ductility by about 20% relative to the baseline, as well as a density reduction of approximately 3–5%.
generation.baseline: The original HfMoTaTiZr HEA, which exhibits a yield strength of approximately 1543 MPa and a fracture strain near 11.6% without the presence of Cr-induced secondary phases.
generation.boundary: These improvements are anticipated at room temperature under laboratory-scale processing conditions; the effects at high temperatures or in bulk-scale components may differ due to processing and scale-dependent factors.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitudes of strength, ductility improvements, and density reduction are subject to variations in processing conditions and microstructural control; the optimal Cr content and exact phase fraction of the Laves phase may require further fine-tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys via vacuum arc melting and homogenization: one baseline HfMoTaTiZr alloy and one alloy with ~4 at% Cr addition along with increased Ti/Zr content. Characterize both alloys using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to identify phase constituents and microstructural features. Conduct room temperature compressive tests to measure yield strength and fracture strain, and determine density via the Archimedes method.
measurements: Yield strength and fracture strain (mechanical compression tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-added alloy does not exhibit a yield strength improvement of at least 150 MPa and a relative ductility increase of >15% over the baseline, or if the measured density reduction is less than approximately 3% compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%.
